newsitem.title: USA: CBOT corn closes lower as Taiwan cancels tenders.
newsitem.headline: CBOT corn closes lower as Taiwan cancels tenders.

text.p: CBOT corn futures closed lower on concerns about lost sales of U.S. corn to Taiwan, traders said.
"We just lost one of our biggest customers and that's going to hurt corn and above all else Taiwan paid cash. There was none of this EEP or loan stuff," a trader said.

Taiwan this week halted exports of pork because of an outbreak of foot and mouth disease in the nation's swine herd. That scenario quickly led to the realization that feed consumption in Taiwan would be reduced and sales of U.S. corn and soybeans to Taiwan would be adversely affected.
Taiwan's Members Feed Industry Group passed on a tender Friday for two shipments of U.S. No. 2 or Argentine corn, traders in Taipei said.

A survey of five major Taiwan grain importers found that all expected significant reductions in corn imports, with most estimating the downturn at about 1.2 million tonnes or 19 percent of the island's annual imports of 6.5 million tonnes.
Corn closed two to 4-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with May down 4-1/2 at $3.00-1/4.
New-crop December corn closed two cents lower at $2.92-3/4 a bushel.

The December gained 2-1/2 cents per bushel relative to its spread with nearby May on bear spreading with persistent talk about potential delays in the seeding of the U.S. corn crop mentioned. That scenario, triggered by a potential wet spring and flooding, could lead to at least a modest shift from corn acres into soybean acres, traders and analysts have said.
Also the bear spreading was tied to some ideas that Taiwan, while temporarily in limbo concerning imports of U.S. corn, could be back in the market in several months.

"We're seeing some bear spreading as a result of this Taiwan news," another trader said. "We will have increased feed demand in the U.S. but it won't show up until the new crop months. Pork producers will increase herds but they can't do it overnight."
Corn futures already were struggling with a late slide in soybeans Tuesday and a sharp break in the soybean market in early dealings Friday.

"A close below $3.00 in May corn and below $8.44 in May beans could spell trouble, at least that's according to technicians I talk to," a trader said. But traders took note that the May closed above three dollars at $3.00-1/4.
Technicians early Friday cited first support in the May at $3.02-3/4 and second support at $2.97-3/4. The session low for May was $2.99.
"This market is stalling against $3.10 (per bushel)," a trader said. "Technical traders are giving up on the breakout." He added that charts suggested a move back to $2.85 per bushel in the May.
First resistance in the May was $3.07-3/4 and second resistance was at $3.12-3/4. The session high for May was $3.02-1/2.
The four- and 20-day moving averages were giving off bullish signals early Friday.
The nine-day relative strength index (RSI) in the May closed at 50-1/2 percent. The market generally considers an RSI of 70 or more as overbought and 30 or less as oversold.

Refco Inc sold six million bushels of May and Rosenthal Collins bought 8.5 million bushels of May, traders said. Cargill Inc bought two million bushels of May and bought 2.5 million bushels of July, traders said. Merrill Lynch Futures sold 2.5 million bushels of July and A.G. Edwards sold 1.2 million bushels of May, traders said.
Corn futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 80,000 contracts, compared with Thursday's volume of 101,571.
In corn options, Term Commodities bought 400 May $3.30 calls at 1-5/8 cents, Tenco Inc bought 200 May $2.90 puts and sold 200 May $3.10 calls at even money, traders said.
Corn options volume was estimated at 19,000, below the 24,983 traded Thursday.
